docs.text: Arizona State University Robotics Engineering and Autonomous Systems Engineer: Jaedyn Harris

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome to my RAS 304 engineering project portfolio!

This website documents the research, design, and development of an Infrared-Based Cliff Detection System using the Vishay TCRT5000 reflective optical sensor.

The purpose of this project is to explore how infrared sensing technology can improve the safety and navigation of autonomous robotic systems.

Throughout this portfolio, I will document the engineering design process, including component selection, circuit calculations, system architecture, and electrical schematic development.

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
Autonomous robots rely on sensors to detect and respond to their surroundings. One important safety challenge is identifying sudden changes in floor elevation, such as stairs, ledges, and drop-offs.

Without an effective detection system, a mobile robot could travel beyond the edge of a supporting surface, potentially damaging its components.

My project focuses on designing a compact and cost-effective infrared cliff detection circuit capable of identifying the presence or absence of a nearby surface.

The system uses the TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensor, which contains both an infrared-emitting diode and a phototransistor.

docs.title: How Does Cliff Detection Work?
docs.text:
The cliff detection system operates using reflected infrared light.

  1. Infrared Emission: The infrared LED emits light toward the ground beneath the robot.

  2. Surface Reflection: When a surface is present, some infrared light reflects toward the phototransistor.

  3. Signal Detection: The phototransistor responds to the reflected light, producing an electrical signal.

  4. Cliff Identification: When the reflected light decreases below a calibrated threshold, the circuit identifies a possible drop-off.

  5. Robot Response: The detection output can be used by a robotic controller to initiate a safety response.

Design Principle: A decrease in reflected infrared light can indicate that the supporting surface is no longer present. Detection reliability depends on sensor positioning, surface reflectivity, and calibration.

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives of this project include:

  • Design an infrared-based cliff detection system.
  • Understand the electrical characteristics of the TCRT5000 sensor.
  • Calculate appropriate resistor values for the infrared LED and phototransistor circuit.
  • Develop a functional system block diagram.
  • Select components based on voltage, current, and power requirements.
  • Create a complete bill of materials (BOM).
  • Design an electrical schematic using KiCad.
  • Document engineering decisions and potential design limitations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Cliff Detection Subsystem is designed to prevent the robot from driving off elevated surfaces. It uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors connected to a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano.

The microcontroller monitors reflected infrared light from the ground and communicates potential cliff hazards to the master controller.

docs.title: Power Source
docs.text:
• 3S Li-ion battery (9–12.6 V) or 9 V bench adapter
  • J1 barrel jack
  • 750 mA fuse (proposed)
  • LM2940CT-5.0 voltage regulator
  • Regulated 5 V power supply
  • USB connection for programming and debugging

The Curiosity Nano's external power connection must be configured according to Microchip's hardware requirements.

docs.text:
Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano

Pin Function RA0 / ANA0 Left TCRT5000 analog input RA1 / ANA1 Right TCRT5000 analog input RD0 Left infrared LED control RD1 Right infrared LED control RB0 UART2 transmit (proposed) RB1 UART2 receive (proposed) GND Common ground

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
The subsystem uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors, positioned on the left and right sides of the robot.

Each sensor contains an infrared LED and phototransistor. The LED emits infrared light toward the ground, while the phototransistor detects reflected light.

The sensor outputs are read through the Curiosity Nano's analog-to-digital converter.

docs.title: Team Interfaces
docs.text:
The subsystem communicates with the master controller through Connector 4 using UART2.

The ribbon cable carries UART transmit, receive, and common ground connections. Exact connector pin assignments must be confirmed with the team.

docs.title: Functional Description
docs.text:
Power enters the subsystem through the J1 barrel jack and passes through fuse protection and a 5 V voltage regulator.

The two TCRT5000 sensors continuously monitor reflected infrared light from the ground.

The Curiosity Nano reads the sensor signals through RA0 and RA1 and compares them against calibrated thresholds.

When either sensor detects a possible loss of ground, the Curiosity Nano sends a cliff warning to the master controller through UART2.

The master controller can then command the motor subsystem to stop or change direction.

docs.title: Part 1: Component Comparison
docs.text: The purpose of the Cliff Detection subsystem is to detect when the robot approaches an edge or drop-off. Three sensors were considered based on cost, sensing capabilities, electrical requirements, and integration with the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

docs.title: 1. TCRT5000 Infrared Reflective Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $1.63

Pros: - Low-cost and readily available. - Compact design with an infrared emitter and phototransistor. - Can detect changes in reflected infrared light. - Simple analog interface with the PIC18F57Q43.

Cons: - Reflectivity changes with floor color and material. - Requires external resistors and signal conditioning. - Sensitive to sensor mounting height and alignment. - Does not directly measure distance.

View TCRT5000 on DigiKey

docs.title: 2. VL6180X-SATEL Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $22.70

Pros: - Measures physical distance rather than reflected light intensity. - Less affected by floor color. - Provides precise distance measurements. - Compact optical sensor.

Cons: - Higher cost than the TCRT5000. - Requires I2C communication. - More complex software integration. - Measurement timing must be considered.

View VL6180X-SATEL on DigiKey

docs.title: 3. VL53L0CXV0DH/1 Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $4.63

Pros: - Measures physical distance using time-of-flight technology. - Less dependent on surface reflectivity. - Compact footprint. - Supports precise distance threshold detection.

Cons: - Requires low-voltage power and compatible logic levels. - Uses I2C communication. - Requires additional software configuration. - Surface-mount package complicates assembly.

View VL53L0CXV0DH/1 on DigiKey

docs.title: Part 2A: Electrical Requirements
docs.text:
The following values were recorded in the initial component comparison.

Component Voltage Current Listed PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 3.3V / 5.0V 50 mA TCRT5000 5.0V 60 mA VL6180X-SATEL 2.8V–5.0V 19 mA VL53L0CXV0DH/1 2.8V–3.3V 19 mA

Important: The TCRT5000's 60 mA value is the infrared LED's absolute maximum continuous forward current, not its required operating current.

The sensor contains two electrically separate components: 1. Infrared LED — requires a current-limiting resistor. 2. Phototransistor — requires a sensing circuit to produce a usable output voltage.

docs.title: Selected Component: TCRT5000
docs.text:
The TCRT5000 was selected for the Cliff Detection subsystem because of its low cost, compact size, and relatively simple electrical interface.

The sensor uses an infrared LED to illuminate the floor and a phototransistor to detect reflected infrared light.

When the robot travels over a reflective surface, infrared light returns to the phototransistor. When the robot approaches an edge, the amount of reflected light decreases. The PIC18F57Q43 can monitor this change and determine whether a possible cliff is present.

Compared with the VL6180X-SATEL and VL53L0CXV0DH/1, the TCRT5000 does not require I2C communication. This simplifies integration with the microcontroller.

The primary disadvantage is sensitivity to different floor materials and colors. Testing and calibration will be required to establish reliable detection thresholds.

docs.title: Integration Plan
docs.text:
1. Supply the infrared LED through a current-limiting resistor.
  2. Connect the phototransistor to an appropriate sensing circuit.
  3. Connect the sensing circuit output to a PIC18F57Q43 ADC input.
  4. Calibrate the reflected-light threshold.
  5. Send a cliff detection signal to the robot's control system when the threshold is crossed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is for my Cliff Detection subsystem board in Project OpenField.

The system uses two TCRT5000 infrared reflective sensors to monitor the ground beneath the left and right sides of the robot. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads the analog sensor signals, determines whether a potential cliff or drop-off is present, and communicates the detection status to the other team subsystems.

The board includes:

  • External DC power input.
  • LM7805 regulated 5V power supply.
  • Two TCRT5000 infrared reflective sensors.
  • Analog signal filtering.
  • Green, yellow, and red status LEDs.
  • Debugging pushbutton.
  • 8-pin ribbon cable communication interface.

Figure 1: Complete Cliff Detection subsystem schematic designed in KiCad. Click the image to enlarge.

Download High-Resolution Schematic PDF

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this power budget is to estimate the electrical power required to operate my TCRT5000 infrared cliff detection circuit.

A power budget is important because it verifies that the selected power supply can deliver sufficient current to all components without exceeding their electrical ratings.

My cliff detection system uses a TCRT5000 reflective optical sensor, consisting of an infrared LED and a phototransistor.

The calculations below estimate current consumption and power requirements for a single sensor circuit operating from a regulated 5V DC supply.

docs.title: Electrical Power Flow
docs.text:
The Cliff Detection subsystem receives power through the external DC barrel jack.

The positive input voltage passes through the 250mA fuse before reaching the LM7805 voltage regulator.

The regulator provides a regulated +5V supply to the Curiosity Nano, sensor pull-up resistors, power indicator LED, and debugging pushbutton.

External DC Power Supply
          |
          v
     J1 Barrel Jack
          |
          v
     F3 250mA Fuse
          |
          v
     LM7805 Regulator
          |
          v
       +5V Rail
          |
          +----> Curiosity Nano VTG
          |
          +----> Green Power LED
          |
          +----> Sensor Pull-up Resistors
          |
          +----> Pushbutton Pull-up

Curiosity Nano Outputs
          |
          +----> RA3 --> Left IR LED
          |
          +----> RA4 --> Right IR LED
          |
          +----> RA5 --> Yellow LED
          |
          +----> RA6 --> Red LED

All circuits share a common ground.

docs.text: J1 Pin Function 1 Positive external DC input 2 Ground 3 Switched connection, unused

docs.title: Voltage Regulator Connections
docs.text:
LM7805 Pin Function Connection 1 Input External voltage through F3 2 Ground Common ground 3 Output Regulated +5V

The LM7805 requires sufficient input voltage above 5V to maintain regulation. A 9V DC input is used as an example for the power calculations.

The actual supply voltage must be confirmed before hardware testing.

docs.title: Bypass Capacitors
docs.text:
Reference Value Purpose C5 0.33 uF Input voltage bypassing C6 0.1 uF Output voltage bypassing

These capacitors help reduce voltage disturbances and provide local bypassing near the regulator.

docs.title: External Curiosity Nano Power
docs.text:
The Curiosity Nano receives external regulated power through its VTG pin.

Pin Connection VTG +5V from LM7805 VOFF GND GND Common circuit ground VBUS No external connection

Connecting VOFF to ground disables the Nano's onboard target voltage regulator.

This allows the microcontroller to operate from the external power supply while USB remains available for programming and debugging.

docs.title: External Power Procedure
docs.text:
1. Connect VOFF to GND.
  2. Connect the external power supply ground.
  3. Apply regulated +5V to VTG.
  4. Connect the USB cable for MPLAB programming if required.

docs.title: USB-Only Operation
docs.text:
To return to USB-only operation, disconnect the external supply from VTG and remove the VOFF-to-GND connection.

A removable jumper may be used to simplify switching between power configurations.

Safety Notes:

  • Do not connect external power to VTG while USB is connected unless VOFF is grounded.
  • Do not connect VOFF to a positive supply voltage.
  • Do not exceed 5.5V on VTG.
  • The external 5V rail must be disconnected or isolated before switching to USB-only operation.

docs.title: TCRT5000 Cliff Detection Sensors
docs.text:
The TCRT5000 is a reflective optical sensor containing an infrared light-emitting diode and a phototransistor.

The infrared LED emits light toward the ground. When a reflective surface is present, some light returns to the phototransistor.

The phototransistor conducts current depending on the amount of reflected infrared light.

The resulting collector voltage is measured by the Curiosity Nano's analog-to-digital converter.

docs.title: Ground Detection
docs.text:
When infrared reflection increases, the phototransistor conducts more current and pulls the collector voltage toward ground.

When reflection decreases, the 10k pull-up resistor raises the collector voltage toward +5V.

Surface Condition Reflected Infrared ADC Voltage Reflective ground Higher Lower Dark ground Lower Higher Cliff or drop-off Usually lower Higher

A high ADC voltage can indicate a potential cliff.

However, dark flooring can produce a similar response. The sensors must be calibrated using different surfaces, mounting heights, and lighting conditions before reliable detection thresholds are selected.

docs.title: Infrared LED Current
docs.text:
Each TCRT5000 infrared emitter uses a 220 Ohm current-limiting resistor.

Assume:

  • GPIO voltage = 5V
  • Infrared LED forward voltage = 1.2V
  • Resistance = 220 Ohms

The current is calculated using Ohm's Law:

I = (V_supply - V_forward) / R

I = (5 - 1.2) / 220

I = 0.01727 A

I = 17.27 mA per sensor

Sensor Estimated Current Left IR emitter 17.27 mA Right IR emitter 17.27 mA Total 34.54 mA

These calculations assume an ideal 5V GPIO output. Actual current depends on the GPIO output voltage and sensor forward voltage.

The microcontroller's GPIO current limits must be verified. External transistor drivers may be required if the GPIO pins cannot supply sufficient current reliably.

docs.title: Resistor Power Dissipation
docs.text:
Power dissipated by each 220 Ohm resistor:

P = I²R

P = (0.01727)² x 220

P = 0.0656 W

P = approximately 66 mW

The selected resistor rating is 0.25W.

Resistor Estimated Operating Power Power Rating 220 Ohms 66 mW 250 mW 1k Ohms 25 mW maximum at 5V 250 mW 10k Ohms 2.5 mW maximum at 5V 250 mW

The selected 1/4W resistors provide adequate power margin for the intended circuit.

docs.title: Pull-up Resistor Current
docs.text:
Each 10k sensor pull-up resistor has a maximum approximate current of:

I = V / R

I = 5 / 10,000

I = 0.5 mA

The combined maximum current for both sensor pull-ups is approximately 1 mA.

docs.title: Analog Signal Filtering
docs.text:
C9 and C11 are 0.1 uF capacitors connected between the sensor collector signals and ground.

Together with the 10k pull-up resistors, they provide approximate RC filtering.

docs.title: RC Time Constant
docs.text:
tau = R x C

tau = 10,000 x 0.0000001

tau = 0.001 seconds

Time Constant = 1 ms

docs.title: Approximate Cutoff Frequency
docs.text:
fc = 1 / (2 x pi x R x C)

fc = 1 / (2 x pi x 10,000 x 0.0000001)

fc = approximately 159 Hz

Parameter Value Resistance 10k Ohms Capacitance 0.1 uF Time constant 1 ms Approximate cutoff frequency 159 Hz

The filtering capacitors help reduce high-frequency noise and short-duration voltage fluctuations.

The actual response depends on phototransistor conductance and ADC loading. Testing is required to ensure the filtering does not delay detection excessively.

docs.title: Analog-to-Digital Conversion
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 uses a 12-bit ADC to convert analog sensor voltages into digital values.

RA0 reads the left sensor.

RA1 reads the right sensor.

Assuming a 5V ADC reference:

ADC Value = (V_input / 5) x 4095

Input Voltage ADC Value 0V 0 1V 819 2V 1638 2.5V 2048 3V 2457 4V 3276 5V 4095

The firmware will compare the measured values with calibrated thresholds to determine whether the robot is approaching a cliff.

The final thresholds will be determined during breadboard and hardware testing.

docs.title: Status LEDs
docs.text:
Three LEDs provide visual feedback during system operation.

LED Color Connection Function D1 Green +5V through R1 System power D5 Yellow RA5 through R7 Left cliff detected D4 Red RA6 through R4 Right cliff detected

Each LED uses a 1k Ohm resistor.

Assuming an LED forward voltage of 2V:

I = (5 - 2) / 1000

I = 3 mA per LED

Operating Condition Green LED Yellow LED Red LED Power On ON OFF OFF Left Cliff ON ON OFF Right Cliff ON OFF ON Both Cliffs ON ON ON

The green LED operates independently of the firmware.

The yellow and red LEDs are controlled by the microcontroller.

docs.title: Electrical Efficiency
docs.text:
The LM7805 is a linear voltage regulator.

It reduces the external input voltage to 5V and dissipates the excess voltage as heat.

Ignoring the regulator's quiescent current, the idealized efficiency is:

Efficiency = (V_output / V_input) x 100%

Input Voltage Output Voltage Idealized Efficiency 7.5V 5V 66.7% 9V 5V 55.6% 12V 5V 41.7%

A lower suitable input voltage reduces the amount of power lost as heat.

docs.title: Example Power Calculation
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Input voltage = 9V
  • Output voltage = 5V
  • Example total load current = 100 mA

Input Power:

P_input = 9 x 0.1

P_input = 0.9W

Output Power:

P_output = 5 x 0.1

P_output = 0.5W

Regulator Power Loss:

P_loss = (9 - 5) x 0.1

P_loss = 0.4W

Efficiency:

Efficiency = (0.5 / 0.9) x 100%

Efficiency = 55.6%

This is an illustrative calculation, not a measured system result. Actual regulator efficiency will be lower when quiescent current is included.

docs.title: Efficiency Improvements
docs.text:
The system could improve energy efficiency by:

  • Activating the infrared emitters only during measurements.
  • Sampling the left and right sensors sequentially.
  • Reducing unnecessary LED operating time.
  • Using microcontroller low-power modes.
  • Selecting a suitable lower input voltage.
  • Replacing the linear regulator with a switching regulator in a future revision.

The current design prioritizes a simple regulated power supply and straightforward debugging.

docs.title: System Operation
docs.text:
The planned operating sequence is:

  1. External DC power enters through J1.
  2. The fuse provides overcurrent protection.
  3. The LM7805 produces regulated +5V.
  4. The green LED indicates system power.
  5. The Curiosity Nano initializes its GPIO and ADC peripherals.
  6. RA3 and RA4 activate the infrared emitters.
  7. RA0 and RA1 read the sensor collector voltages.
  8. The firmware compares the ADC readings with calibrated thresholds.
  9. The yellow or red LED activates if a potential cliff is detected.
  10. The detection status is communicated to the MASTER board.
  11. The system repeats the sensing process.

docs.title: Detection Logic
docs.text:
Left Sensor Right Sensor Intended Response Ground Ground Continue normal operation Cliff Ground Yellow LED and left cliff status Ground Cliff Red LED and right cliff status Cliff Cliff Both LEDs and hazard status

The robot's motion controller should respond to a confirmed hazard by stopping or avoiding the drop-off.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• All resistors are rated at 1/4W.
  • The input fuse is rated at 250mA.
  • The fuse uses two Keystone 3512 clips for a 5x20mm cartridge.
  • The system operates from a regulated 5V supply.
  • C9 and C11 are rated at 16V.
  • C5 and C6 should have voltage ratings appropriate for the final supply voltage.
  • Sensor filtering capacitors should be placed near the analog input connections.
  • Regulator bypass capacitors should be placed near the LM7805.
  • Analog traces should be kept away from noisy digital signals.
  • A common ground plane should be used when possible.
  • The Curiosity Nano footprint must match the actual development board.
  • The TCRT5000 footprints must match the physical sensor terminal positions.
  • The sensors must be oriented toward the ground.
  • Sensor mounting height must be verified experimentally.
  • UART logic voltage compatibility must be checked with the team.

docs.title: Electrical Rules Check
docs.text:
The latest documented KiCad ERC results are:

Check Result Errors 0 Warnings 2

The remaining warnings are related to differences between the custom Curiosity Nano and LM7805 schematic symbols and their saved library versions.

The custom symbols and footprints must be verified before PCB manufacturing.

A successful ERC does not independently verify current limits, mechanical fit, thermal performance, or firmware behavior.

docs.title: Breadboard Verification
docs.text:
The following tests are planned to verify the operation of the Cliff Detection subsystem.

Test Expected Result Status LM7805 Output Approximately 5V Planned Green LED Illuminates with regulated power Planned Left Sensor ADC voltage changes with reflection Planned Right Sensor ADC voltage changes with reflection Planned Left Cliff Detection Yellow LED activates Planned Right Cliff Detection Red LED activates Planned Pushbutton RA7 changes HIGH to LOW Planned UART Communication Correct data transmitted and received Planned Current Consumption Within system power budget Planned Regulator Temperature Within safe operating limits Planned

docs.title: Testing Procedure
docs.text:
1. Verify the regulator output voltage before connecting the Nano.
  2. Confirm that VTG receives regulated 5V.
  3. Verify VOFF and common ground connections.
  4. Test each infrared emitter independently.
  5. Measure the collector voltage at RA0 and RA1.
  6. Test multiple ground colors and surface materials.
  7. Test different sensor mounting heights.
  8. Determine reliable cliff detection thresholds.
  9. Verify the status LED responses.
  10. Test the ribbon cable communication interface.
  11. Measure total system current and regulator temperature.

Measured voltages, current consumption, and calibrated ADC thresholds will be recorded after hardware testing.
